Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Michael Vance had not stepped into a trench without feeling the ground give way since the day he watched a load of rebar collapse at the Meridian commercial site. He was standing twenty feet away when the shoring plates buckled. What stayed with him were not the sounds so much as the still frames that kept cycling behind his eyes: a yellow hard hat tipping forward, a sudden plume of gray dust catching the afternoon sun, boots scuffing against concrete as a coworker was pulled down. When the memory returns, it does not whisper; it arrives as a full picture. Along with the images come the smells of damp clay and diesel exhaust, thick enough to coat his throat. He tastes the same gritty, metallic dust that had settled on his lips that afternoon, a sharp flavor that lingers long after the moment passes. In the weeks following the collapse, Michael had come to believe that the ground beneath him was no longer reliable. His beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, replaced by a quiet certainty that bad things could arrive without warning, no matter how carefully he planned or where he stood. He found himself inadequate, as though he should have been able to brace the structure or pull his colleague clear, even though the engineering logs later showed the failure was sudden. Helplessness settled over him next. He could not stop bad things from happening to him; they simply arrived, and he was left to absorb them. His symptom inventory sat at seventy-three, a number that mirrored the quiet weight he carried. To navigate the days, Michael adopted strategies that made sense to him. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger, keeping it locked behind his ribs. On the job site, he turned to the card tables at the VFW hall. He gambled to distract himself or feel excitement. When the site grew loud, he stepped back to his truck. He deliberately tried to leave his body or blank out. He would roll down the window and let the concrete sounds of the construction environment fade into a dull hum, his thoughts drifting somewhere above the scaffolding. The habits formed over weeks and months. He began avoiding the southern trench where the collapse had occurred, taking a longer route through the staging area even when it delayed his shift. The crew noticed his quiet withdrawal, and the distance between him and his wife had widened before the divorce was finalized. He hesitated near heavy machinery, and he stopped attending the company gatherings, preferring to eat alone while the memories of dust and diesel played out behind his eyes. His anger remained suppressed, his gambling steady, and his deliberate dissociations frequent, all moving through his days without any one of them necessarily pushing the others forward. Now, at thirty-nine, Michael sits in a therapist’s office with his boots still caked in dried site mud. What finally brought him here was the quiet accumulation of a life held at arm’s length. He is not sure the world will ever feel solid again, and he fears another collapse will catch him off guard. What he hopes for, he admits with a slow exhale, is a way to stay present when the pictures return, to taste the dust without losing himself, and to walk through a trench without wondering when the ground might give way.
